body_markdown:
The neurology landscape has become increasingly dynamic over the past decade. As amyloid targeting therapies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders advance, the industry's focus has shifted away from PET imaging to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and more recently, blood-based biomarkers of amyloid and Tau pathology. For drug developers, biomarkers are no longer supplementary research tools. They are becoming essential components of clinical development strategies, patient selection and therapeutic decision-making.


## From CSF to the Blood-Based Biomarker Revolution


CSF biomarkers have transformed AD research by providing a more scalable and cost-effective approach to disease stratification and pathology assessment than amyloid PET imaging. Early advances in automated testing led to regulatory approval of three ratio tests (Aβ42/Aβ40, pTau181/Aβ42 ratio, Aβ42/tTau) that strongly correlate with amyloid PET positivity which enabled more sustainable, practical and consistent measurement of disease pathology.
Today, the most significant shift in neuro drug development is the regulatory approval of blood-based biomarkers of neuropathology that offer a less invasive, even more scalable approach for clinical trials and, ultimately, routine clinical practice.


For sponsors, these advances can improve trial efficiency by reducing recruitment barriers, lowering operational burden and helping identify patients earlier in the disease continuum. As biomarker-driven clinical trials become more common, blood-based testing is poised to become central to both patient selection and therapeutic development.

## Key Trends Driving Clinical Development Today


While individual biomarkers remain important, the field quickly explored ratio tests (e.g. Aβ 42/40) with the addition of the second analyte normalizing individual variation, improving accuracy and reducing false readings of AD associated biomarker significantly. Today, sponsors are evaluating combinations of biomarkers that not only indicate the presence of a specific pathology (amyloid, Tau, synuclein, TDP43) but also capture other distinct aspects of disease biology, including contributions by glial cells, vascular dysfunction, synaptic health and neurodegeneration.


This trend reflects a broader evolution of our understanding of neurodegenerative diseases as complex and multifactorial, often presenting with overlapping symptoms, common biomarkers and shared pathologies. Expanded biomarker frameworks are helping researchers differentiate between closely related diseases and develop a more comprehensive picture of disease progression and treatment response. To handle intricate data sets, potentially across various omic platforms, increasingly complex algorithms will be needed to reduce noise, combine and magnify signals, and recognize patterns. Unsurprisingly, assay standardization remains critical to harmonize testing results across platforms, sites and studies and to support regulatory acceptance.


Finally, while amyloid and tau remain foundational biomarkers of amyloid pathology in AD, tau pathology correlates more closely with synaptic loss, hippocampal atrophy, and cognitive decline. Biomarkers such as eMBTR Tau-243 and pTau205 correlate much better with Tau PET positivity and cognitive decline and can help monitor disease progression and treatment response. While not yet approved for patient management, these and other biomarkers are attracting significant interest for their potential to stage AD progression more accurately.


## What Comes Next?


While AD biomarker research has advanced rapidly, other indications, including Parkinson's disease, still lack robust biomarkers. Dopa decarboxylase (DDC) has emerged as a promising CSF biomarker, and sponsors continue to seek markers that differentiate related diseases, stratify patients, and track specific pathological processes. To this end, acetylated α-synuclein, acetylated Tau174/tTau, TDP-43 cryptic peptides, integrins, and 14-3-3 proteins are being investigated.


Technology innovations are also accelerating discovery. For example, ultrasensitive proteomic platforms can now detect low-abundance proteins at attomolar concentrations, expanding protein profiling capabilities. Other assays for extracellular vesicles and miRNAs would further expand the repertoire of neurology biomarkers, although technical and biological challenges remain.


## Partnering for the Future of Neuroscience


As neuro drug development becomes more biomarker intensive, success depends on access to clinically validated assays, standardized testing strategies and scientific and regulatory expertise across the development lifecycle. From early biomarker discovery through clinical trial implementation and patient stratification and monitoring, Labcorp offers a partnership that can help sponsors translate emerging science into actionable strategies.


The future of neuroscience will be defined by better differentiation between related diseases and monitoring of pathology and therapeutic response. Patient selection will rely on multiple biomarkers that match pathological mechanisms with therapeutic mechanisms of action. Organizations that invest now in integrated biomarker strategies will be best positioned to accelerate timelines, reduce risk and deliver meaningful outcomes for patients living with neurodegenerative diseases.


## About the authors:


### Dr. Roland Staal, Director, Scientific Engagement Neurology, Labcorp


Dr. Staal is a seasoned leader in neuroscience drug discovery and translational research with over 20 years of experience spanning academia, biotech, and pharmaceuticals. He has led research programs in Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, neuropathic pain, Rett syndrome, ALS, stroke, and mitochondrial disorders. His career includes leadership roles at Pfizer, Lundbeck, and Lucy Therapeutics, where he established pioneering research capabilities and advanced multiple therapeutic programs. He has also founded a biotechnology company and served as a strategic advisor to universities, biotech and foundations, on drug discovery, translational strategies, and business strategy. With over 20 years of experience in neurology, drug discovery and translational strategies, Roland brings deep expertise to Labcorp and its clients.


### Dr. Magali Dupont, Lead Scientist, Immunology, Labcorp


Dr. Dupont holds a PhD in Immunology from the Institut Pasteur in Paris and joined the Immunology department at Labcorp Central Laboratory Services in 2021. In her role, she oversees validation work performed at the central laboratory in Geneva, Switzerland, addresses scientific operational challenges and investigates new biomarkers and methodologies to ensure high-quality scientific delivery.


With the increased focus on biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases, Dr. Dupont has led the validation and operationalization of several assays and platforms to support clinical trials, as well as acquired valuable functional experience, allowing Labcorp to offer multiple approaches to support neurobiomarker testing.


### Dr. Satya Narla, Senior Scientific Director, Core Automated Testing /Immunology/Special Chemistry/Vaccines


Dr. Narla joined Labcorp in January 2016 as a senior scientist in the immunology department and and has since held positions of increasing responsibility within scientific and operational leadership. She received her PhD in clinical bioanalytical chemistry from Cleveland State University in 2013 and completed her postdoctoral training as clinical chemist from the Medical University of South Carolina.


In her current role, she provides scientific and technical leadership to laboratory teams and clients, helping drive innovation, assay development, and the implementation of new testing capabilities. She partners closely with internal and external stakeholders to support complex scientific inquiries, advance laboratory solutions, and ensure the delivery of high-quality data. She has authored multiple peer-reviewed publications, including three book chapters, and has contributed to numerous scientific presentations and posters.
